questions.question: In computer memory systems, a Virtually Indexed, Physically Tagged (VIPT) L1 cache can potentially suffer from cache aliasing (where multiple virtual addresses map to different cache sets but refer to the same physical address). What hardware design relationship completely guarantees that aliasing cannot occur without requiring software page coloring?
options: The total cache capacity divided by its associativity must be less than or equal to the virtual memory page size.
The cache must be fully associative so that set index bits are eliminated entirely from the cache lookup.
The physical address tag width must be strictly greater than the sum of the cache index bits and line offset bits.
The cache associativity must be an integer multiple of the number of page table levels implemented by the MMU.
The cache must implement a write-through policy rather than a write-back allocation policy.

questions.question: In modern out-of-order superscalar microarchitecture design, why do high-performance processors overwhelmingly favor an explicit Unified Physical Register File (PRF) organization over the classic scheme where the Reorder Buffer (ROB) itself stores speculative result values?
options: The PRF scheme completely eliminates the need for branch misprediction checkpointing and recovery logic.
The PRF scheme allows data values to be written once into a single dedicated register array, eliminating redundant data copying and wide data buses across the Reorder Buffer and issue queues.
The PRF scheme allows speculative load instructions to execute out-of-order without requiring address checks against uncommitted stores.
The PRF scheme completely eliminates the need for speculative Register Alias Tables (RAT) in the instruction decode stage.
The PRF scheme enforces in-order execution of arithmetic operations while allowing out-of-order execution only for memory accesses.

questions.question: When designing a multi-stage flip-flop synchronizer to transfer a single-bit asynchronous signal across Clock Domain Crossing (CDC) boundaries, which relationship accurately captures the Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) caused by flip-flop metastability?
options: MTBF is inversely proportional to the resolution time available to the synchronizing latch, scaling as exp(-T_resolve / tau).
MTBF increases linearly with the source data transition frequency and the receiving clock frequency: MTBF proportional to f_clk * f_data.
MTBF is proportional to exp(T_resolve / tau) / (f_clk * f_data), where T_resolve is available settling time and tau is the flip-flop regenerative time constant.
MTBF is independent of clock frequency and determined solely by the supply voltage and flip-flop setup time.
MTBF scales as (tau / T_resolve) * log(f_clk * f_data), describing logarithmic improvement with increasing settling time.

questions.question: In synchronous digital integrated circuit design and clock distribution network analysis, what is the fundamental distinction between 'clock skew' and 'clock jitter'?
options: Clock skew is a dynamic cycle-to-cycle phase noise at a single pin, whereas clock jitter is a static routing mismatch across different clock domains.
Clock skew affects only setup time constraints, whereas clock jitter affects only hold time constraints.
Clock skew can be entirely eliminated using on-chip Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs), whereas clock jitter cannot be filtered by phase locked circuitry.

Clock skew is the spatial variation in arrival times of a clock edge at two different sequential elements during the same cycle, whereas clock jitter is the temporal variation in arrival time at a given clock sink across successive cycles.
Clock skew is caused solely by dynamic power supply noise (di/dt), whereas clock jitter is caused exclusively by static RC interconnect delay mismatch.

questions.question: In nanoscale CMOS device physics and low-power IC design, what fundamental physical mechanism dictates the 'Boltzmann tyranny', setting a lower limit of approximately 60 mV/decade on the subthreshold swing (SS) of conventional MOSFETs at room temperature (300 K)?
options: Direct quantum-mechanical tunneling of carriers from the source to the drain through the thin channel barrier.
The saturation of drift velocity caused by optical phonon scattering under high lateral electric fields.
Gate dielectric leakage current arising from Fowler-Nordheim field emission across the high-k oxide.
Band-to-band tunneling (BTBT) occurring across the reverse-biased drain-to-body junction under high supply voltages.
The thermal Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distribution tail of carriers crossing the channel electrostatic potential barrier via thermionic emission.
